lead: Encapsulation means an object keeps its data to itself and lets the outside world reach it only through methods. Abstraction means those methods promise what they do, not how. Together they keep a class safe to change: a caller cannot push an impossible value into an object, and the class can rewrite its insides without breaking any caller. Every Python library you use — a UPI payment object, a datetime, a pandas DataFrame — is built this way. This chapter covers the three visibility levels, accessors and mutators, validation, and @property.
prereq: You need: classes and objects (4.1) and the self keyword and __init__ (4.2).

blocks.text: Encapsulation bundles an object's data with the methods that use that data, and hides the data from outside code. The object's state is written only by its own methods. Callers ask for what they need through methods. Creating attributes and methods is in 4.1.
Python has no enforced private fields. It has three naming levels that every Python reader interprets the same way.

Written as
What Python does
rows: nothing special; readable and writable from anywhere
nothing special; a convention meaning internal, do not touch

blocks.text: The double underscore is called name mangling. Inside class Temperature, the line self.__celsius = 25 is rewritten by Python to self._Temperature__celsius = 25 before the code runs. This is a rename, not a lock: reading t._Temperature__celsius from outside works fine. The rename exists so that a subclass reusing the same attribute name does not accidentally overwrite the parent's data.
A single underscore is a promise, a double underscore is a rename, and neither is a security feature. That is why Python encapsulation is called encapsulation by convention.
An accessor, or getter, is a method that returns one attribute. A mutator, or setter, is a method that changes one attribute. Some syllabi call mutators setters; the two words mean the same thing.

Why not let callers write t.celsius = 25 directly? Because plain assignment cannot refuse a bad value. The lowest possible temperature is -273.15 °C, absolute zero. A setter can check that rule before storing.

items: Store the value in a private attribute: self.__celsius = 0 in __init__.
Write def set_celsius(self, value): and put the check first: if value < -273.15: raise ValueError("below absolute zero").
Only after the check passes, assign: self.__celsius = value.
Callers use only these two methods, never the attribute.

blocks.text: Order matters. If you assign first and check afterwards, the bad value is already inside the object when the exception is raised, and the object is left in an impossible state.
The figure follows two calls on one object. set_celsius(25) passes the check and stores 25. set_celsius(-300) fails the check, raises ValueError, and leaves the stored 25 untouched.
Writing get_x and set_x for every attribute is noisy. The @property decorator lets a method be used like an attribute: t.celsius = 25 instead of t.set_celsius(25).

Two rules make properties work. The setter is registered with @celsius.setter, where celsius must match the getter's name exactly. A property with only the getter is read-only: t.celsius = 30 then raises AttributeError.

Abstraction shows the caller what a method does and hides how. len(my_list) returns a count; you neither know nor care whether Python reads a stored length or loops. t.set_celsius(25) guarantees a valid temperature; the caller never sees __celsius, the check, or the mangled name.

The public methods of a class form its interface. Everything behind them — private attributes, helper methods, the internal layout — can be rewritten next month and no caller notices. That freedom is the practical payoff of encapsulation plus abstraction.
Abstract base classes push the idea further by forcing subclasses to supply certain methods; see 4.7. Inheritance itself is in 4.4.

figure.caption: The setter checks before it stores: 25 °C passes and is written, while -300 fails, raises ValueError, and the stored 25 stays. Notice that a rejected call never changes the object.

spec.title: Validated setter
spec.aria: A client calls set_celsius(25), which passes the -273.15 check and stores 25; set_celsius(-300) fails, raises ValueError, and the stored 25 stays.

examples.question: Define a class Temperature whose private attribute __celsius starts at 0. set_celsius(value) must raise ValueError when value < -273.15 and otherwise store it; get_celsius() returns the stored value. Create t = Temperature(), call t.set_celsius(25) and print get_celsius(). Then call t.set_celsius(-300) inside a try/except ValueError, and print get_celsius() again. State both printed lines and the name under which the attribute is actually stored.
steps: t = Temperature() runs __init__, so the attribute is created as _Temperature__celsius = 0.
t.set_celsius(25): the check is 25 < -273.15, which is false, so the check passes.
t.get_celsius() returns 25; the first printed line is 25.
t.set_celsius(-300): the check is -300 < -273.15, which is true, so ValueError("below absolute zero") is raised.
No assignment happens; except ValueError catches the error and the stored value is still 25.
t.get_celsius() returns 25 again; the second printed line is 25.
Inside the class the source says __celsius; outside, name mangling makes it _Temperature__celsius.
examples.answer: Both printed lines are 25: the rejected call -300 leaves the stored temperature at 25 °C, and the real attribute name is _Temperature__celsius.

traps: Believing t.__celsius from outside reads the private value. It does not; you must write t._Temperature__celsius.
Writing t.__celsius = -300 at module level does not raise an error. It creates a brand new attribute named __celsius, bypassing validation entirely, while get_celsius still returns the old 25.
Putting the assignment before the check: the invalid value is stored, then ValueError is raised, and the object is left broken.
Thinking @property alone makes an attribute read-only for good. A getter plus @name.setter is read-write; only a bare getter raises AttributeError on assignment.
Mixing up the two words: encapsulation hides the data, abstraction hides the working. Expect a one-mark definition question on this.

quiz.q: What does Python do to the attribute name __price written inside class Item?
quiz.a: It renames it to _Item__price. This is name mangling; it is a rename, not private storage.

quiz.q: Why should a class expose set_celsius(value) instead of letting callers assign the attribute directly?
quiz.a: The setter can validate the value before storing it, keeps the rule in one place, and lets the class change its internal representation later without breaking callers.
The call set_c(30) stores 30. set_c(-500) fails the check and raises ValueError, which is caught, so nothing is stored. The output is 30.

quiz.q: A student writes the setter as: self.__celsius = value, then if value < -273.15: raise ValueError. What is wrong with this order?
quiz.a: The check comes after the assignment, so the invalid value is already stored when the exception is raised. The object stays in an impossible state. The check must run before the assignment.

quiz.q: A class defines celsius as a property with a getter only. What happens when outside code runs t.celsius = 25?
quiz.a: Python raises AttributeError, because a property without a setter blocks assignment. Reading t.celsius still works.

quiz.q: Why is self._price not protection at all?
quiz.a: The single underscore is only a convention. Python applies no rename and no check, so any code can read or overwrite t._price freely.

quiz.q: Give one reason a library author keeps an attribute private and offers get_celsius() instead of a public attribute.
quiz.a: So the storage can change later, for example from Celsius to Kelvin internally, while get_celsius() still returns Celsius. The interface stays fixed and no caller code breaks.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real Python libraries lean on @property and on plain attributes with documented rules, not on deep private trees. Data classes and the attrs package generate validated attributes automatically, and typing tools such as mypy flag writes to a read-only property at check time. The idea you should carry forward is the interface: design the small set of public methods first, then let everything else be private and free to change. Search for 'Python property decorator', 'name mangling' and 'dataclasses field validation' when you want more.
